lead: A corpus is a fixed, cleaned, documented collection of real text, gathered so that every later model is trained and compared on the same data. Without one, two teams report accuracy on different sentences and neither number means anything. Sources include plain text, HTML pages, PDFs, subtitles, newspaper archives, government portals, Wikipedia dumps, public web crawls and speech transcripts. Only a few universities teach corpus building as a named topic, yet every project in this unit starts here.
prereq: You need the normalization and tokenization decisions of Chapter 1.4, because extracted text must be cut into tokens before any count is meaningful.

blocks.text: A corpus starts from text a computer can read. Plain .txt is simplest. HTML hides text inside markup. PDFs store glyph positions, so extraction may reorder words. Subtitles come as timed blocks. Wikipedia dumps and public web crawls, such as Common Crawl, arrive already packaged. Speech transcripts first need a recognizer, whose errors enter your corpus.

Permission comes before code. Copyright protects expression, not facts. Check the licence. robots.txt at a site root lists paths a crawler should avoid for a given User-agent; it is a convention, not a law, and ignoring it can get your address blocked. Terms of service may forbid scraping. Personal data such as names, phone numbers and identity numbers must be removed or never collected. Institutional ethics approval may be required before storing text about people.

items: Send one request every few seconds, not ten at once.
Identify your crawler in the User-agent header.
Honour Retry-After and cache pages so a rerun does not hit the server again.

sections.h3: From a URL to clean text

items: Pick URLs from sitemaps or link lists and record each one.
Fetch with a delay and store the raw HTML.
Parse HTML with a parser, never with a regular expression.
Select content elements: article, main, headings.
Extract text, decode as UTF-8, unescape entities.
Drop boilerplate: menus, footers, ads, cookie notices.
Remove near-duplicates: split each document into 5-word shingles, hash them, compare Jaccard overlap.
Split into train, development and test.

blocks.text: A shingle is a contiguous run of 5 tokens from a document. Two documents are compared by Jaccard overlap = |A ∩ B| ÷ |A ∪ B|, where A and B are their shingle sets. Values near 1 mean near-duplicates.

Split first. Any threshold a cleaning step needs, such as a language-filter score, must be chosen on training documents only. Steps that need no threshold, such as boilerplate removal, may run on all documents. Near-duplicates must be removed before the split; otherwise a copy of a test document sits in training and inflates the score.

Store one document per line in JSONL, with fields id, url, date and text. A CSV with a text column works for small corpora. Plain files need a manifest listing filename, source, licence and split. Record the random seed and the split counts. Vocabulary size is the number of distinct word types, counted after normalization such as lowercasing. Because the same words repeat across a corpus, it is much smaller than the token count: 208,000 tokens may come from only a few thousand types. Some syllabi add word association measures, pointwise mutual information PMI(w₁,w₂) = log₂[P(w₁,w₂)/(P(w₁)P(w₂))] and the t-score, to rank collocations; see Unit 5.

spec.title: Building a corpus
spec.aria: A top to bottom flow from a list of URLs through fetching with a robots.txt check, parsing HTML, extracting text, cleaning and deduplicating, to a corpus file.

examples.question: You scrape 400 pages at an average of 650 words per page. Each word takes 5 characters plus 1 space in storage. Find the word-token count and the raw size in MB. Boilerplate removal then deletes 20 percent of the words; find the remaining tokens and size. Use 1 MB = 1,000,000 characters.
examples.answer: The raw corpus has 260,000 word tokens and 1.56 MB; after boilerplate removal it has 208,000 word tokens and 1.248 MB.
examples.check:
pages = 400
words_per_page = 650
chars_per_word = 5
space = 1
total_words = pages * words_per_page
raw_chars = total_words * (chars_per_word + space)
raw_mb = raw_chars / 1_000_000
kept = 0.8 * total_words
kept_chars = kept * (chars_per_word + space)
kept_mb = kept_chars / 1_000_000
print(f'raw tokens = {total_words}')
print(f'raw characters = {raw_chars}')
print(f'raw size = {round(raw_mb, 2)} MB')
print(f'kept tokens = {int(kept)}')
print(f'kept characters = {int(kept_chars)}')
print(f'kept size = {round(kept_mb, 3)} MB')
examples.output:
raw tokens = 260000
raw characters = 1560000
raw size = 1.56 MB
kept tokens = 208000
kept characters = 1248000
kept size = 1.248 MB

traps: Counting HTML tags as text; tags inflate the vocabulary with fake tokens such as div and span.
Ignoring robots.txt and request rate limits, then wondering why the server blocks your address.
Deduplicating after the train and test split, so near-copies of test documents sit in training.
Confusing word-token count with vocabulary size; 208,000 tokens may come from only a few thousand distinct word types.
Decoding UTF-8 bytes as Latin-1 and storing mojibake without noticing.

quiz.q: What is robots.txt and what does it contain?
quiz.a: A file at a site root with User-agent and Disallow lines, telling crawlers which paths to avoid.

quiz.q: Why split into train, development and test before tuning a language filter?
quiz.a: Tuning on test data leaks test information, so the reported score is too high.

quiz.q: You scrape 300 pages of 700 words each; a word takes 5 characters plus 1 space. Boilerplate removal deletes 10 percent. Find tokens, raw MB and kept MB.
Two documents have 5-word shingle sets of sizes 120 and 100, with 20 shingles shared. Compute Jaccard overlap and say whether they are near-duplicates.
quiz.a: Jaccard = 20 ÷ (120 + 100 − 20) = 20 ÷ 200 = 0.10. That is low overlap, so they are not near-duplicates.

quiz.q: Why must boilerplate be removed before counting words?
quiz.a: Menus, footers and cookie notices repeat on every page, so they inflate counts and teach the model site layout rather than content.

quiz.q: Name two storage formats for a corpus and one field each should hold.
quiz.a: JSONL with one document per line holding id, url, date, text; or CSV with a text column.

beyond: Not for the exam. Large projects store raw crawls as WARC files and deduplicate with MinHash or SimHash at billion-page scale. Data cards record source, licence, date and known biases. Search terms: Common Crawl, WARC, MinHash deduplication, data card, corpus manifest.
